Failed Role suggests a strong role-based or responsibility-based meaning of the trauma, but the rest of the profile does not indicate injury-related incapacity, inability to work, or family-protector themes that would support this appraisal. For this patient, it feels insufficiently grounded in the surrounding items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Permanent humiliation' is not impossible after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation and item set, which otherwise centers on fear-based post-collision threat, sensory reliving, and vulnerability rather than shame/humiliation. It is the least clinically integrated appraisal here and is hard to explain without other supporting shame-related items.

'Entrapment: Having no options' is not a clear contradiction, but for this trauma/profile it is weakly integrated compared with the other trigger items. The rest of the profile emphasizes crash reminders, reliving, danger appraisals, and hyperarousal. A strong entrapment trigger would usually be better supported by appraisals or memory content about being trapped or unable to escape, which are absent here.

vignette:
Thomas was sixty-seven, a school principal of thirty-four years, when his life veered into a ditch. Driving home on a wet November evening, a sedan ran a red light and T-boned his driver-side door. The impact accordioned the frame; he was trapped for twenty minutes, conscious through the crunch of metal and the hiss of steam. In the hospital, the doctors called him lucky-bruised ribs, a fractured wrist, no internal bleeding-but Thomas did not feel lucky. He felt hollowed out, as though the crash had snapped something inside him that could not be mended. That feeling grew roots in the weeks that followed, flowering into a quiet certainty: somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. He replayed the moment of impact over and over, a film that ran unbidden, and when it ran he felt the steering wheel against his chest again, the breath knocked out of him. The memory came not in words-he could never seem to put the frightening event into language-but in images and sensations that made the present moment dissolve. He was certain he had permanently changed for the worse, and every new day confirmed that the world was a dangerous place. Having concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was no longer the same man, staying home from work felt not like avoidance but like the only rational choice.

That felt truth shaped everything. Because Thomas believed the world was dangerous, he began to read danger into small delays: when a meeting ran five minutes late, his stomach tightened because he assumed something bad was happening. Already running on threat, he found that almost anything could tip into a warning-a car door slamming in the parking lot, a student's laughter rising too fast, the flicker of a brake light at the intersection ahead. He could not relax even in his own living room, certain that safety was an illusion. The belief that he was permanently damaged made him watchful for any sign that the crash had broken him, and that watchfulness kept the memory alive-every time he felt his body tense, the film started again. He also found that the same belief sharpened his ears to specific triggers: shouting, which had once been the normal noise of a school hallway, now made him flinch because it sounded like the paramedics yelling; loud noises of any kind-a dropped tray in the cafeteria, a slammed door-sent him back behind the wheel; and any car that had been hit, even a minor fender-bender in the parking lot, became an image he could not look away from.

Those triggers, in turn, yanked him straight into the memory. A student shouting in the corridor, and suddenly Thomas was not in the corridor: he was in the crushed car, the airbag powder in his throat, the film playing frame by frame. The reliving was so vivid that he felt the event happening right now, his heart pounding, his palms slick.

Faced with that onslaught, Thomas developed strategies that made sense to him but kept the loop turning. He began to avoid going to work-his own school, his own building-because the hallways were too full of shouting, and the parking lot was too full of cars. He told himself he was just taking a few sick days, but the days stretched into weeks. When he did force himself to go in, he found that the avoidance had only made the triggers more jarring, and the memory more intrusive. At home, he tried to drown the film with positive thoughts-I'm safe, it's over, everything is fine-but the forced reframing felt hollow, and after an hour of suppressing the memories he would find himself standing in the kitchen, eating cereal straight from the box, eating until his stomach ached, because the fullness was the only thing that quieted the replay. The overeating left him sluggish, which made it harder to relax, and the guilt that followed-I'm eating myself into a heart attack-only deepened his conviction that he had permanently changed for the worse. He kept telling himself that a better person would have bounced back by now, but he could not, and that failure made him watch for danger even more.

The threat itself became a fertile ground. His trouble falling asleep meant he lay in the dark replaying the crash, the memory feeding the threat, the threat feeding the memory. When something took longer than expected-a traffic light, a doctor's appointment-he felt the world closing in, and that tension directly reinforced his belief that nowhere was safe. The threat also drove him back to his strategies: after a night of broken sleep he would stay home from work again, and after a day of staying home he would eat to soothe the restlessness. And those strategies, in turn, fed the threat: avoiding work made him feel incompetent and more exposed when he finally returned, and overeating left him breathless, which he interpreted as a sign that something bad was happening.

By the time his wife insisted he see a psychologist, Thomas had been out of work for three months. The school board was growing impatient; his assistant principal was running the building. What finally brought him through the door was not insight but exhaustion. He was tired of the loop. He was afraid that if he did not get help, he might never go back to the job he had loved, and he was even more afraid that the crash had changed him so thoroughly that nothing could bring him back.
